newsitem.title: UK: Teddy bear, ex-lover won't stop old Thatcher ally.
newsitem.headline: Teddy bear, ex-lover won't stop old Thatcher ally.

text.p: Alan Clark must be the the only candidate in the British election to face an ex-lover, her cuckolded husband and a teddy bear on his political comeback trail.

The past has come back to haunt the flamboyant millionaire, better known for his rumbustious diaries and irrepressible libido than for his eight years as a Conservative minister under Margaret Thatcher.

Retired judge James Harkess, who once said Clark should be horsewhipped for sleeping with his wife and her two daughters, has flown half way across the world from South Africa to canvass for the opposition Labour Party against Clark.
Harkess, who insisted his motive was not revenge, said: "We all sin but there is no need to do it in serial fashion."

His wife Valerie was aghast at the warm reception given to Clark in London's elegant Kensington and Chelsea constituency, which ranks as one of the safest Conservative seats in the May 1 general election.
"Are they so jaded that they've got to be amused by a man who is nearly an old age pensioner, who seduced my daughters and who had an affair with me?," she asked on arrival.
But the harsh words cut no ice with Clark as the sprightly 69-year-old bounds into a supermarket to charm "blue rinse matrons" in silk scarves, tweed skirts and gold buckle shoes.
"You're the handsome one," said one old lady delightedly chucking him under the chin by the fruit and vegetable counter.

This is the heart of affluent London and Clark, who bitterly regretted leaving parliament five years ago, is in his element. His old constituency was a downtrodden area of a naval port, Plymouth, but Kensington and Chelsea is much more his style.
His wife, who has been long on suffering and forgiveness over the years, mocks Clark for wheeling a shopping trolley around. "It's not his job -- but it won't do him any harm."
Clark is the great survivor in an era when a string of Conservative ministers have resigned in sex scandals.
He has provided fodder for Britain's voracious tabloids ever since the 1993 publication of racy diaries in which he alluded to the triple seduction of what he called "the coven."
When the Harkesses sold their story to a Sunday newspaper, Jane Clark witheringly commented "Quite frankly, if you bed people of below-stairs class, they go to the papers."
Out on the campaign trail, any mention of the Harkess family is met with world-weary resignation by the Clarks.
Clark, whose hugely entertaining diaries have outsold the weighty memoirs of his former boss Thatcher, told Reuters: "I have never commented.
"It was a very long time ago, the episodes to which they are referring. They came over three years ago, had a huge media circus and were, I understand, rewarded very handsomely."
Apart from Labour, Clark is facing a candidate from the Teddy Bear Alliance Party which is standing on a "Vote for a Flea-Free Britain" platform. Clark is not amused.

"I am not all that keen on silly season politics. I think it slightly trivialises it," he said before being hailed by bevies of carefully coiffeured ladies. They greet him coyly like a raffish bounder they have cornered at a cocktail party.
There is no mistaking the renewed zest shown by Clark, who inherited much of his 40 million pound ($60 million) fortune, lives in a 12th century castle and loves fast cars and fine wines.
But has he reformed? Sir David Frost recently asked him on television if he had relinquished wine, women and song. Clark said he had never been particularly addicted to song.
